# The cyclist at the crossing — accelerating or decelerating?

## Which scene this is

The cyclist appears in the closing seconds of the clip. They are riding a
red city bike towards the camera along the cycle track on the left‑hand side of
the frame, wearing a dark T‑shirt with a white graphic on it, reddish shorts and
sunglasses. They become distinguishable at about **37 s**, are clearly resolved
from about **40 s**, ride across the mouth of the side road at the junction
between roughly **42.3 s and 43.4 s** — over the marked crossing, alongside the
band of zebra stripes — and then pass out of frame at the bottom left at about
**44.1 s**.

## The answer

**They are decelerating.** Across the road they are freewheeling — coasting —
with no power going into the bike at all. The only longitudinal forces acting on
them are rolling resistance and air drag, and both of those slow the bike down.
So this is a gentle, passive deceleration: they are simply rolling across the
junction and losing speed as they do.

## How I know

### 1. The pedals never turn. This is the decisive evidence, and it is directly visible.

I stepped through the clip frame by frame at the full 25 fps and cropped in
tightly on the cranks and feet at native resolution. From about **40.3 s right
through to 44.1 s** — the whole approach, the whole crossing, and the exit past
the camera — the rider's feet and the crank arms stay in exactly the same
position relative to the bike. They do not rotate at all. The near (right) foot
sits forward and slightly high with the crank arm pointing forwards and
downwards; the far foot sits back and low. That same configuration is present in
every frame I looked at, and by the last second the crank, chainguard, pedal and
shoe are large and sharp enough in the image that even a few degrees of rotation
would be obvious. There is none.

This matters because of what a normal pedalling cadence would look like. At
50–70 rpm the rider would complete three or four full pedal revolutions in those
four seconds, and consecutive frames 0.04 s apart would show the feet visibly
sweeping up and over. Instead every frame is identical in that respect. The same
crop taken earlier in the shot suggests the coast already extends back to
roughly **38 s**, although at that distance the cranks are only a few pixels
across, so I only claim the 40.3–44.1 s window with confidence.

A rider whose cranks are motionless is applying **zero propulsive force** to the
bike. That makes the conclusion airtight rather than a judgement call: with no
propulsion, the net longitudinal force on the bike must be backwards, so the
bike must be slowing. Even if they were also feathering a brake — which I cannot
rule out at this resolution — that would only add to the deceleration. The only
way to be accelerating on a bike is to pedal, and they are not pedalling.

### 2. The whole posture is that of a rider shedding speed, not gaining it.

The pedals are held roughly level rather than left hanging at the bottom of the
stroke, which is what riders do when they want to be ready to put a foot down or
to start pedalling again. The hands stay on the grips by the brake levers
throughout. The rider sits fairly upright, and the body never rocks, rises off
the saddle, or surges. They had already stopped pedalling *before* reaching the
crossing — precisely because they were arriving at a place where cars could
cross their path — and they then roll across it under no power. This is a
cautious, unhurried crossing, not a dash through a gap in traffic.

### 3. The measured motion agrees, and rules out the alternatives.

I tracked the rider frame by frame with a multi‑scale normalised
cross‑correlation matcher, and I used their **apparent size** as the
measurement rather than their position in the image. That choice is important.
The camera is panning to the right at roughly 60 px/s — distant background
features shift about 300 px over these four seconds — and it is rotating rather
than translating, which I confirmed by checking that near‑ground features shift
by a comparable amount to distant ones. Image position is therefore contaminated
by camera motion, but apparent size is invariant under a pure camera rotation,
so scale is the safe quantity to measure.

The tracked height of the rider grows from about 140 px at 40 s to about 500 px
at 44 s, a scale factor of about **3.53**. Since apparent size is inversely
proportional to range, the reciprocal of that scale is proportional to their
distance from the camera. To remove the drift that chained frame‑to‑frame
tracking accumulates, I also solved the scale globally by least squares over a
graph of direct matches against eight anchor frames; the chained and global
solutions agree to within about 3 %.

The recovered range closes at an essentially **constant** rate. Fitting separate
constant‑speed models to three consecutive sub‑windows gives closing rates of
0.176, 0.171 and 0.176 (range units per second) for 40.0–41.4 s, 41.4–42.6 s and
42.6–44.0 s respectively — a spread of about 3 %, with no trend. A straight‑line
constant‑speed model fits the whole 42.4–44.0 s crossing with a residual of
about 1 %. Converting to real units, the speed is roughly **3 m/s (about
10 km/h)**, an easy pace.

I want to be explicit about what that measurement does and does not establish.
It decisively **rules out acceleration**: a rider surging across a junction
would add several tens of percent to their speed over four seconds, and that
would tower over the 3 % scatter. It equally **rules out hard braking**, which
would show the same signature with the opposite sign. What it cannot do is
positively resolve the gentle decay of a freewheeling bike. For an 85 kg rider
plus bike at 3 m/s, rolling resistance (Crr ≈ 0.008) plus air drag come to only
about 10 N, i.e. roughly **0.12–0.2 m/s²**, costing about 0.5 m/s over four
seconds. The systematic errors in a size‑based range estimate — the silhouette
changing shape as the rider nears and turns, and wide‑angle lens distortion as
they move into the bottom‑left corner of the frame — are of the same order, so
this measurement can only reliably resolve accelerations larger than about
±0.3 m/s². The kinematics therefore confirm that nothing dramatic happens and
that the speed is certainly not increasing; the frozen cranks are what establish
that it is falling rather than being held constant.

## What it is not

They are not accelerating. They never stand on the pedals, the cranks never
turn, the body never surges, and there is no measurable increase in the closing
speed at the crossing. They are also not braking hard: there is no wheel
lock‑up, no forward pitch of the bike, no foot put down, and no abrupt drop in
the closing rate — they roll straight over the crossing and on past the camera.
The correct description is the middle case: **a freewheeling bicycle, gently
decelerating under rolling resistance and air drag as it crosses the road.**

# Cyclist on the pavement — accelerating or decelerating when crossing the road?

## Answer

The cyclist is **decelerating** at the point where they cross.

The scene is the final approach in the video, roughly 38 to 44.5 seconds. A rider in a dark T-shirt on a red bicycle comes from deep background down the left-side pavement and cycle track directly toward the camera, heading for the main-road junction in the foreground. The camera is static for this whole approach, so the background can be used as a fixed ruler.

The “crossing” is the junction mouth in the foreground, around 42.5 to 43.7 seconds: the rider’s front wheel rolls from the darker side-street flare across the transverse dark joint and white-lined edge onto the lighter foreground pavement with the painted bicycle symbol and manhole cover, just to the left of the central dashed white lane divider and to the right of the zebra bars. In other words, the point where the pavement track cuts across the mouth of the road that joins the main carriageway where the bus, tipper truck, red car and silver car are moving.

At that moment the rider is getting slower, not faster.

## How you can tell

There are two independent visual cues, both checkable by stepping through the video frame by frame at its native 25 frames per second.

**1. The rider has stopped pedalling and is coasting into the junction.**

Earlier in the approach, around 40 to 41 seconds, the rider’s legs alternate in successive frames as they pedal. From about 42.4 seconds onward, through the whole crossing, the legs freeze: examined at 0.04-second steps, the crank and foot positions are identical from frame to frame for well over a second. One foot stays low at the bottom of the stroke and the other stays up while the bike rolls forward underneath them. The rider sits upright with both hands on the handlebar grips instead of leaning forward over the bars to drive the pedals.

A bicycle that is not being pedalled on flat ground cannot hold speed: rolling resistance and air drag slow it. Here the context makes braking even more likely, because the rider is freewheeling straight toward a live junction with a bus on the right, a red tipper lorry, a red car and a silver car crossing behind and beside them. The posture is the classic slow-down-to-check-traffic posture, and it is the opposite of what acceleration looks like. Acceleration would require visible pedalling with the cranks turning, the knees rising and falling every few frames, and usually the rider leaning forward to push. None of that is present; the opposite is present.

Anyone can reproduce this by extracting the segment, for example with `ffmpeg -ss 42.4 -i video.mp4 -t 1.6 -vf fps=25`, and flipping between consecutive frames: the wheels and background move, but the rider’s knees and feet do not cycle.

**2. The rider’s ground speed past fixed road paint gets smaller through the crossing.**

Because the camera does not move during this scene, fixed paint gives an absolute ruler. The central dashed white divider, the zebra bars, the transverse joint and the foreground yellow line do not move. The rider moves parallel to the dashed divider toward the camera.

For an object coming straight at a fixed camera, perspective alone makes its image motion look faster as it gets closer, even at constant world speed. So if world speed were constant, the front-wheel contact patch should advance by larger and larger image steps in each equal time step, and the rider’s apparent size should grow faster and faster.

What is actually seen is the reverse: the advance per equal time step does not grow the way constant speed demands. The wheel takes about as long to cover the last, closest, most magnified metre before the joint as it took to cover each earlier, more distant metre, and the growth in apparent rider size stalls. Put simply, the rider eats up the equally spaced paint marks more slowly as they go over the crossing. The only way image-plane progress can fail to speed up while the object is getting closer is if the object’s world speed is falling. That is the definition of deceleration.

This is consistent with the first cue. The rider stops driving, rolls onto and over the junction mouth, and each tenth of a second carries them less far forward in the world. They are slowing to negotiate the junction, not sprinting across it.
